claim: Cortical function critically depends on inhibitory/excitatory balance.
source: Cortical function critically depends on inhibitory/excitatory balance.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cortical function.

claim: Cortical inhibitory interneurons (cINs) are born in the ventral forebrain and migrate into cortex.
source: Cortical inhibitory interneurons (cINs) are born in the ventral forebrain and migrate into cortex, where their numbers are adjusted by programmed cell death.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cIN development.

claim: cIN numbers are adjusted by programmed cell death.
source: Cortical inhibitory interneurons (cINs) are born in the ventral forebrain and migrate into cortex, where their numbers are adjusted by programmed cell death.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cIN development.

claim: Loss of clustered gamma protocadherins (Pcdhg), but not of genes in the alpha or beta clusters, increased dramatically cIN BAX-dependent cell death in mice.
source: Here, we show that loss of clustered gamma protocadherins (Pcdhg), but not of genes in the alpha or beta clusters, increased dramatically cIN BAX-dependent cell death in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Electrophysiological and morphological properties of Pcdhg-deficient and wild-type cINs during the period of cIN cell death were indistinguishable.
source: Surprisingly, electrophysiological and morphological properties of Pcdhg-deficient and wild-type cINs during the period of cIN cell death were indistinguishable.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Co-transplantation of wild-type with Pcdhg-deficient interneuron precursors further reduced mutant cIN survival.
source: Co-transplantation of wild-type with Pcdhg-deficient interneuron precursors further reduced mutant cIN survival, but the proportion of mutant and wild-type cells undergoing cell death was not affected by their density.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data from co-transplantation experiments.

claim: The proportion of mutant and wild-type cells undergoing cell death was not affected by their density.
source: Co-transplantation of wild-type with Pcdhg-deficient interneuron precursors further reduced mutant cIN survival, but the proportion of mutant and wild-type cells undergoing cell death was not affected by their density.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data from co-transplantation experiments.

claim: Pcdhgc3, Pcdhgc4, and Pcdhgc5 play a critical role in regulating cIN survival during the endogenous period of programmed cIN death.
source: We conclude that Pcdhg, specifically Pcdhgc3, Pcdhgc4, and Pcdhgc5, play a critical role in regulating cIN survival during the endogenous period of programmed cIN death.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study supported by experimental data from transplantation assays.

claim: The ratio of inhibitory interneurons to excitatory neurons is crucial for establishing and maintaining proper brain function.
source: The ratio of inhibitory interneurons to excitatory neurons is crucial for establishing and maintaining proper brain function (Rossignol, 2011; Chao et al., 2010; Marín, 2012; Hattori et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2007; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Alterations in the number of cINs have been linked to epilepsy.
source: Alterations in the number of cINs have been linked to epilepsy (Dudek and Shao, 2003), schizophrenia (Beasley and Reynolds, 1997; Hashimoto et al., 2003; Enwright et al., 2016) and autism (Gao and Penzes, 2015; Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Fatemi et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Alterations in the number of cINs have been linked to schizophrenia.
source: Alterations in the number of cINs have been linked to epilepsy (Dudek and Shao, 2003), schizophrenia (Beasley and Reynolds, 1997; Hashimoto et al., 2003; Enwright et al., 2016) and autism (Gao and Penzes, 2015; Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Fatemi et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Alterations in the number of cINs have been linked to autism.
source: Alterations in the number of cINs have been linked to epilepsy (Dudek and Shao, 2003), schizophrenia (Beasley and Reynolds, 1997; Hashimoto et al., 2003; Enwright et al., 2016) and autism (Gao and Penzes, 2015; Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Fatemi et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During mouse embryonic development, the brain produces an excess number of cINs and ~40% of those are subsequently eliminated by apoptosis during early postnatal life, between postnatal day (P)1 and 15.
source: During mouse embryonic development, the brain produces an excess number of cINs and ~40% of those are subsequently eliminated by apoptosis during early postnatal life, between postnatal day (P)1 and 15 (Southwell et al., 2012; Denaxa et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: cINs are generated in the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences (MGE; CGE) of the ventral forebrain.
source: In normal development, cINs are generated in the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences (MGE; CGE) of the ventral forebrain, far from their final target destination in the cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cIN development.

claim: cINs migrate tangentially from their site of origin to reach the neocortex, where they become synaptically integrated and complete their maturation.
source: cINs migrate tangentially from their site of origin to reach the neocortex, where they become synaptically integrated and complete their maturation (Anderson et al., 1997; Wichterle et al., 2001; Butt et al., 2005; Nery et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ganglionic eminences are an important source of interneurons in the developing human brain, where migration and differentiation extend into postnatal life.
source: The ganglionic eminences are also an important source of interneurons in the developing human brain, where migration and differentiation extend into postnatal life (Hansen et al., 2013; Paredes et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activity-dependent mechanisms regulate cIN survival through their connectivity to excitatory neurons.
source: While recent work suggests that activity-dependent mechanisms regulate cIN survival through their connectivity to excitatory neurons (Wong et al., 2018; Denaxa et al., 2018; Duan et al., 2020; Priya et al., 2018) studies indicate that cIN survival is mediated by a population-autonomous (or cell-autonomous) mechanism (Southwell et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: cIN survival is mediated by a population-autonomous (or cell-autonomous) mechanism.
source: While recent work suggests that activity-dependent mechanisms regulate cIN survival through their connectivity to excitatory neurons (Wong et al., 2018; Denaxa et al., 2018; Duan et al., 2020; Priya et al., 2018) studies indicate that cIN survival is mediated by a population-autonomous (or cell-autonomous) mechanism (Southwell et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Heterochronically transplanted MGE cIN precursors undergo a wave of apoptosis coinciding with their age, which is asynchronous from endogenous cINs.
source: Heterochronically transplanted MGE cIN precursors undergo a wave of apoptosis coinciding with their age, which is asynchronous from endogenous cINs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal survival in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is regulated through limited access to neurotrophic factors secreted by target cells.
source: Whereas it is well established that neuronal survival in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is regulated through limited access to neurotrophic factors secreted by target cells (Huang and Reichardt, 2001; Aloe and Chaldakov, 2013; Oppenheim and Carolanne, 2013), cIN survival is independent of TrkB, the main neurotrophin receptor expressed by neurons of the CNS (Southwell et al., 2012; Rauskolb et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: cIN survival is independent of TrkB, the main neurotrophin receptor expressed by neurons of the CNS.
source: Whereas it is well established that neuronal survival in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is regulated through limited access to neurotrophic factors secreted by target cells (Huang and Reichardt, 2001; Aloe and Chaldakov, 2013; Oppenheim and Carolanne, 2013), cIN survival is independent of TrkB, the main neurotrophin receptor expressed by neurons of the CNS (Southwell et al., 2012; Rauskolb et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The proportion of cINs undergoing apoptosis remains constant across graft sizes that vary 200-fold.
source: Moreover, the proportion of cINs undergoing apoptosis remains constant across graft sizes that vary 200-fold (Southwell et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: cIN developmental death is intrinsically determined and cell-autonomous mechanisms within the maturing cIN population contribute to the regulation of their survival.
source: Taken together, this work suggests that cIN developmental death is intrinsically determined and that cell-autonomous mechanisms within the maturing cIN population contribute to the regulation of their survival.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The clustered protocadherins (Pcdh) are a set of cell surface homophilic-binding proteins implicated in neuronal survival and self-avoidance in the spinal cord, retina, cerebellum, hippocampus, and olfactory bulb glomeruli.
source: The clustered protocadherins (Pcdh) (Wu and Maniatis, 1999) are a set of cell surface homophilic-binding proteins implicated in neuronal survival and self-avoidance in the spinal cord, retina, cerebellum, hippocampus, and olfactory bulb glomeruli (Ing-Esteves et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2002b; Lefebvre et al., 2012, Lefebvre et al., 2008; Katori et al., 2017; Mountoufaris et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the mouse, the Pcdh locus encodes a total of 58 isoforms that are arranged in three gene clusters, alpha, beta and gamma: Pcdha, Pcdhb, and Pcdhg.
source: In the mouse, the Pcdh locus encodes a total of 58 isoforms that are arranged in three gene clusters, alpha, beta and gamma: Pcdha, Pcdhb, and Pcdhg (Wu et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Pcdha and Pcdhg isoforms are each composed of a set of variable exons, which are spliced to three common constant cluster-specific exons.
source: The Pcdha and Pcdhg isoforms are each composed of a set of variable exons, which are spliced to three common constant cluster-specific exons (Tasic et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Each variable exon codes for the extracellular, transmembrane and most-proximal intracellular domain of a protocadherin protein.
source: Each variable exon codes for the extracellular, transmembrane and most-proximal intracellular domain of a protocadherin protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protocadherin structure.

claim: The Pcdhb isoforms are encoded by single exon genes encoding both extracellular, transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains.
source: The Pcdhb isoforms are encoded by single exon genes encoding both extracellular, transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains (Wu and Maniatis, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A combinatorial, yet stochastic, set of isoforms is expressed in each neuron.
source: Of the 58 Pcdh genes, it has been suggested that a combinatorial, yet stochastic, set of isoforms is expressed in each neuron (Esumi et al., 2005; Kaneko et al., 2006; Mountoufaris et al., 2017), suggesting a source for neuronal diversity in the CNS (Canzio et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pcdhg genes, and specifically isoforms Pcdhgc3, Pcdhgc4, and Pcdhgc5, are required for the postnatal survival of mice.
source: Interestingly, Pcdhg genes, and specifically isoforms Pcdhgc3, Pcdhgc4, and Pcdhgc5, are required for the postnatal survival of mice (Wang et al., 2002b; Hasegawa et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RT-PCR analysis revealed the expression of each of the 58 isoforms in the Pcdh gene locus in the adult cortex (P30).
source: RT-PCR analysis revealed the expression of each of the 58 isoforms in the Pcdh gene locus in the adult cortex (P30) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pcdhg genes are essential for postnatal survival.
source: Of the 58 Pcdh genes, those in the Pcdhg cluster are essential for postnatal survival (Hasegawa et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2012), and are implicated in cell death in the retina and spinal cord (Lefebvre et al., 2008; Prasad et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pcdhg genes are implicated in cell death in the retina and spinal cord.
source: Of the 58 Pcdh genes, those in the Pcdhg cluster are essential for postnatal survival (Hasegawa et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2012), and are implicated in cell death in the retina and spinal cord (Lefebvre et al., 2008; Prasad et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: With the exception of Pcdhga9 isoform, all other 21 Pcdhg were detected in cINs.
source: With the exception of Pcdhga9 isoform, we detected the expression of all other 21 Pcdhg in cINs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All eight isoforms (Pcdhgc3, Pcdhgc4, Pcdhgc5, Pcdhga1, Pcdhga2, Pcdhga3, Pcdhgb6, and Pcdhgb7) were expressed in cINs at P2, P5, P8, P12 and P15.
source: All eight isoforms were expressed in cINs at each of the five ages studied.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expression of Pcdhgc5 increased dramatically between P8 and P15.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Pcdhgc5 increased dramatically between P8 and P15.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An increase in expression of Pcdhg isoforms Pcdhga1, Pcdhga2 and PcdhgC4 was observed at P12, compared to other ages.
source: An increase in expression of Pcdhg isoforms Pcdhga1, Pcdhga2 and PcdhgC4 was also observed at P12, compared to other ages, but this increase was less pronounced than that observed for Pcdhgc5.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All Pcdh isoforms are expressed in cINs.
source: The above results show that all Pcdh isoforms are expressed in cINs and that the expression of Pcdhg isoforms Pcdhga1, Pcdhga2 and PcdhgC4 and Pcdhgc5 increases during the period of postnatal cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RT-PCR and qPCR data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The expression of Pcdhg isoforms Pcdhga1, Pcdhga2 and PcdhgC4 and Pcdhgc5 increases during the period of postnatal cell death.
source: The above results show that all Pcdh isoforms are expressed in cINs and that the expression of Pcdhg isoforms Pcdhga1, Pcdhga2 and PcdhgC4 and Pcdhgc5 increases during the period of postnatal cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the qPCR data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Most cINs are produced between embryonic days (E) 10.5 and 16.5 by progenitors located in the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences (MGE and CGE).
source: Most cINs are produced between embryonic days (E) 10.5 and 16.5 by progenitors located in the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences (MGE and CGE) (Anderson et al., 1997; Wichterle et al., 2001; Nery et al., 2002; Miyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Robust GFP expression was detected throughout the brain in E13.5 embryos, including cells in the MGE and CGE.
source: Robust GFP expression was detected throughout the brain in E13.5 embryos, including cells in the MGE and CGE (Figure 3B), indicating expression of Pcdhg isoforms in cIN progenitors.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pcdhg isoforms are expressed in cIN progenitors.
source: Robust GFP expression was detected throughout the brain in E13.5 embryos, including cells in the MGE and CGE (Figure 3B), indicating expression of Pcdhg isoforms in cIN progenitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GFP expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice displayed growth retardation after birth.
source: However, homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14 ;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice displayed growth retardation after birth, a hind limb paw-clasping phenotype when held by the tail and were infertile (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice displayed a hind limb paw-clasping phenotype when held by the tail.
source: However, homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14 ;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice displayed growth retardation after birth, a hind limb paw-clasping phenotype when held by the tail and were infertile (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice were infertile.
source: However, homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14 ;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice displayed growth retardation after birth, a hind limb paw-clasping phenotype when held by the tail and were infertile (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Brain size as well as cerebral cortex thickness of homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 was similar to those of control mice.
source: Brain size as well as cerebral cortex thickness of homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 was similar to those of control mice (Figure 2B').
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by measurements shown in Figure 2B'.

claim: The density of tdTomato positive cells in somatosensory and visual cortex was roughly halved in homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 animals, compared to wild type and heterozygous littermates.
source: However, the density of tdTomato positive cells in somatosensory and visual cortex was roughly halved in homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 animals, compared to wild type and heterozygous littermates (Figure 2C and C').
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 2C and C'.

claim: The density of cINs stained positive for parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SST) (MGE-derived), vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP )(CGE-derived) or reelin (RLN) (derived from both the MGE and CGE) was significantly reduced in the visual cortex of homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice.
source: The density of cINs stained positive for parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SST) (MGE-derived), vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP )(CGE-derived) or reelin (RLN) (derived from both the MGE and CGE) was significantly reduced in the visual cortex of homozygous Gad2Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The embryonic loss of Pcdhg function in GABAergic progenitor cells leads to a drastically reduced number of cINs in the neocortex, affecting all cIN subtypes similarly.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that the embryonic loss of Pcdhg function in GABAergic progenitor cells leads to a drastically reduced number of cINs in the neocortex, affecting all cIN subtypes similarly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Homozygous Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 embryos lost GFP expression specifically in in the MGE and the preoptic regions.
source: Homozygous Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 embryos lost GFP expression specifically in in the MGE and the preoptic regions (Figure 3B), consistent with full recombination and loss of Pcdhg function in cells derived from the Nkx2.1 lineage.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At P30, the number of MGE-derived tdTomato+ cells in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice was dramatically reduced (~50%) in both the visual and somatosensory cortex.
source: At P30, the number of MGE-derived tdTomato+ cells in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice was dramatically reduced (~50%) in both the visual and somatosensory cortex (Figure 3C and C').
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 3C and C'.

claim: MGE-derived PV and SST interneuron number was similarly reduced in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 animals.
source: MGE-derived PV and SST interneuron number was similarly reduced in these animals.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CGE-derived VIP interneuron density was similar to that of control animals in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice.
source: However CGE-derived VIP interneuron density was similar to that of control animals (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A smaller, but significant reduction in the RLN positive cIN population was observed in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice.
source: A smaller, but significant reduction in the RLN positive cIN population was observed, in agreement with the notion that a subpopulation of RLN cells is born in the MGE (Miyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Layer 1 RLN+ cells, which are largely derived from the CGE, were not affected by Pcdhg loss of function.
source: Consistently, layer 1 RLN+ cells, which are largely derived from the CGE (Miyoshi et al., 2010), were not affected by Pcdhg loss of function, but RNL cells in deeper layers 2–6 (many of which are MGE-derived and also positive for SST) showed reduced numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: RNL cells in deeper layers 2–6 (many of which are MGE-derived and also positive for SST) showed reduced numbers in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice.
source: Consistently, layer 1 RLN+ cells, which are largely derived from the CGE (Miyoshi et al., 2010), were not affected by Pcdhg loss of function, but RNL cells in deeper layers 2–6 (many of which are MGE-derived and also positive for SST) showed reduced numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice, the number of un-recombined PV and SST (PV+/tdTomato- and SST+/tdTomato-) cells was significantly increased compared to WT mice.
source: Interestingly, we observed that in our Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice, the number of un-recombined PV and SST (PV+/tdTomato- and SST+/tdTomato-) cells was significantly increased compared to WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), a result consistent with recent observations (Carriere et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: PV+/tdTomato- and SST+/tdTomato- cells are likely derived from the most dorsal MGE at the interface with LGE expressing NKX6.2 in a region of low, or no expression of NKX2.1.
source: PV+/tdTomato- and SST+/tdTomato- cells are likely derived from the most dorsal MGE at the interface with LGE expressing NKX6.2 in a region of low, or no expression of NKX2.1 (Hu et al., 2017a; Hu et al., 2017b; Fogarty et al., 2007; Sousa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Embryonic loss of Pcdhg function in Nkx2.1-positive progenitors results in a significant reduction in the number of MGE/POA-derived cINs.
source: Together the above results show that embryonic loss of Pcdhg function in Nkx2.1-positive progenitors results in a significant reduction in the number of MGE/POA-derived cINs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The reduction in the number of cINs in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice was not a result of abnormal cortical thickness or abnormal layer distribution.
source: The reduction in the number of cINs in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice was not a result of abnormal cortical thickness or abnormal layer distribution, as these measures were similar across genotypes in P30 mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The number of dividing cells in the ventricular or subventricular zones at E13.5 and E15.5 showed no difference in the number of mitotic cells in the MGE between Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14; Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice and controls.
source: Quantification of the number of dividing cells in the ventricular or subventricular zones at E13.5 and E15.5, using the mitotic marker Phosphohistone H3 (PH3), showed no difference in the number of mitotic cells in the MGE between Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14; Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice and controls (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell counts shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Migration of young cINs into cortex was not affected in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice.
source: Migration of young cINs into cortex was also not affected in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 mice .
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell counts shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The tdTomato+ cells in the cortex displayed a similar migratory morphology in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 embryos and controls.
source: The tdTomato+ cells in the cortex displayed a similar migratory morphology in Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 embryos and controls.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The number of migrating cells in cortex in the marginal zone (MZ), the subplate (SP), and the intermediate and subventricular zone (IZ/SVZ) was equivalent between Pcdhg mutant embryos and controls at E15.5.
source: Consistent with the absence of an effect of Pcdhg on cIN migration, the number of migrating cells in cortex in the marginal zone (MZ), the subplate (SP), and the intermediate and subventricular zone (IZ/SVZ) was equivalent between Pcdhg mutant embryos and controls at E15.5 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell counts shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Loss of Pcdhg did not affect the proliferation of MGE progenitors or the migration of young MGE-derived cINs into the developing neocortex.
source: These findings indicate that loss of Pcdhg did not affect the proliferation of MGE progenitors or the migration of young MGE-derived cINs into the developing neocortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: A wave of programmed cell death eliminates ~40% of the young cINs shortly after their arrival in the cortex.
source: A wave of programmed cell death eliminates ~40% of the young cINs shortly after their arrival in the cortex (Southwell et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This wave starts at ~P0, peaks at P7, and ends at ~P15.
source: This wave starts at ~P0, peaks at P7, and ends at ~P15.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the timing of cIN cell death.

claim: Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 homozygous mice displayed a wave of programmed cell death peaking at P7.
source: Similarly to their wild type littermates, Nkx2.1Cre;Ai14;Pcdhgfcon3/fcon3 homozygous mice displayed a wave of programmed cell death peaking at P7 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell death measurements shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Pcdhg mutant mice had significantly higher numbers of tdTomato+/CC3+ cells compared to controls.
source: However, Pcdhg mutant mice had significantly higher numbers of tdTomato+/CC3+ cells compared to controls.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell death measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: With the exception of a small, but significant increase observed at P0, there was no significant difference in the number of CC3+/tdTomato- cells between genotypes.
source: With the exception of a small, but significant increase observed at P0, we found no significant difference in the number of CC3+/tdTomato- cells between genotypes (Figure 5B, bottom graph).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell death measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The survival of neighboring Pcdhg-expressing cells is not impacted by the loss of Pcdhg-deficient MGE/POA-derived cINs.
source: This suggests that the survival of neighboring Pcdhg-expressing cells is not impacted by the loss of Pcdhg-deficient MGE/POA-derived cINs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell death measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The homozygous deletion of the pro-apoptotic Bcl-2-associated X protein (BAX) rescued cIN density in the Pcdhg mutant mice to levels similar to those observed in control Bax-/- ;Pcdhfcon3/+ mice or in mice carrying only the Bax mutation (Bax-/-).
source: Importantly, the homozygous deletion of the pro-apoptotic Bcl-2-associated X protein (BAX) rescued cIN density in the Pcdhg mutant mice to levels similar to those observed in control Bax-/- ;Pcdhfcon3/+ mice or in mice carrying only the Bax mutation (Bax-/-) (Southwell et al., 2012; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by cell density measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of Pcdhg in MGE/POA-derived cIN enhances their demise through programmed cell death during the developmental period when these cells are normally eliminated.
